title: Victim Warns Of Microsoft Tech Support Scam
description: Thousands of people across the Country are falling victim to a scam where people will pose as Microsoft tech support employees when in reality they are working to scam people out of their money.

asr.full_text: Scammed out of hundreds, if not thousands of dollars by someone claiming to be a Microsoft employee. That's what many victims are saying happened to them. And News Channel 5's Jessie Knudson spoke to a victim who said she's speaking out so others won't lose out on their cash. I really felt stupid at the time for falling for such a thing. This scam all started when Harriet got an email saying her computer was infected and that she needed to call a Microsoft representative at a provided number. They were telling me different things that were going wrong with my computer and how they could help me. People all around the country have been told the same thing. Their computer is infected, but they can get help for a couple hundred dollars. They knew all the moves. To pull up all those things on my computer and show me what was infected, that really was, oh, I've got to do something now. Harriette paid about $200 and was told everything was fixed. And then the scammers came back for more. They called me and said the Better Business Bureau said they were going to have to close down because their computers were infected. They said they were going to refund her money, but then proceeded to show her a screen saying they refunded too much, nearly $2,000. It even showed up in a fake statement. And it said it was deposited to our bank account. They asked Harriet to pay it back using gift cards, which she did, but that money she received was never there, according to her bank. If I received a deposit for 1999 and they're going no The Better Business Bureau says you should avoid using gift cards to pay for services. That is a major red flag. These types of payments generally you can't get your money back and scammers know that. Instead they suggest you go to a known vendor for help with electronics and other issues. That way you can avoid being a victim of one of these scams. Out of every one consumer report that they receive, there is approximately 50 more consumers that we have not heard from. Harriet received a total of 43 phone calls from these scammers and was constantly harassed. And she hopes that by speaking out about it, no one else will fall victim.

textual.observation: A reported email claimed that the viewer's computer was infected, directed her to call a purported Microsoft representative, and led to a request for payment for computer assistance.

evidence.quote: This scam all started when Harriet got an email saying her computer was infected and that she needed to call a Microsoft representative at a provided number.
Their computer is infected, but they can get help for a couple hundred dollars.

textual.context: Presented as a victim account in a news report warning others; the source attributes the account to Harriet and does not establish the identity of the caller.
textual.potential_relevance: The reported Microsoft identity claim and infection warning are linked to a requested call and a payment for assistance, which may require later assessment of the offer and affiliation.
textual.limitations: The records do not independently verify the email, caller, Microsoft affiliation, computer condition, or payment outcome.

textual.observation: A reported caller said that money had been refunded in excess and requested repayment of the alleged excess using gift cards.

evidence.quote: They said they were going to refund her money, but then proceeded to show her a screen saying they refunded too much, nearly $2,000.
They asked Harriet to pay it back using gift cards, which she did

textual.context: Presented as a victim's reported experience within a news report; the source describes the alleged refund and repayment request rather than independently verifying them.
textual.potential_relevance: A claimed refund and overpayment is directly linked to a request to transfer value through gift cards, a relationship that may require later assessment of the payment mechanism and stated refund.
textual.limitations: The records do not establish whether any refund or deposit occurred, who controlled the payment process, or the identity of the callers.

visual.observation: News segment graphics state “TECH SUPPORT SCAMS” and “VICTIM WARNS OF FAKE MICROSOFT TECH SCAM.”
visual.context: Visible TV news warning/reporting context with a Channel 5 logo and anchor on screen.
visual.potential_relevance: The on-screen wording links a claimed Microsoft-related tech support identity to a warning about a fake tech support scenario, which conditionally merits review as a reported identity/support claim rather than as proof from the frames alone.
visual.limitations: The sampled frames do not show the full report, any caller identity details, or whether Microsoft branding appeared in the underlying communication.

visual.observation: A warning-style pop-up graphic says “YOUR COMPUTER MAY BE INFECTED,” claims personal and financial information is “NOT SAFE,” and instructs the viewer to call tech support now at a partially blurred 866 number.
visual.context: Shown within a TV news segment warning about fake Microsoft tech support and gift-card payment warnings; the phone number is partially obscured.
visual.potential_relevance: The visible pop-up combines an urgent computer infection/data-safety claim with a requested action to call a toll-free tech support number, a concrete mechanism discussed in the warning context.
visual.limitations: The frames do not establish who created the pop-up, whether the number was contacted, or any resulting transaction or data disclosure.

visual.observation: A printed example of a computer warning includes “WARNING! YOUR COMPUTER MAY BE INFECTED,” a partially visible [PHONE] number, and a “Clean Now!” button-like label.
visual.context: Displayed in a news/reporting context with lower-third text “SCAMS GO UNDERREPORTED.”
visual.potential_relevance: The printout visibly links an infection warning to prompts to call a support number or use a clean-now action, matching a concretely described tech-support warning mechanism in the report context.
visual.limitations: The frame does not show an actual live website interaction or whether anyone clicked, called, paid, or provided information.

visual.observation: Lower-third text states “SCAM CAN COST VICTIMS THOUSANDS OF DOLLARS” while an interview subject appears on screen.
visual.context: Visible interview/news context about the alleged tech support scam impact.
visual.potential_relevance: The report visually connects the discussed tech-support scam scenario with a possible monetary loss amount in the thousands, preserving the warning/reporting framing.
visual.limitations: The sampled frames do not show the specific payment method, recipient, amount paid by the interview subject, or documentation of loss.

visual.observation: A phone screen shows repeated missed calls listed as “No Caller ID,” while the lower third says “BBB WARNS AGAINST USING GIFT CARDS FOR PAYMENTS.”
visual.context: Visible news warning context referencing BBB guidance; no specific caller or payment demand is shown in the frame.
visual.potential_relevance: The frame links unsolicited/unknown caller activity with a warning about gift cards as a payment method, a concretely described payment-related scam mechanism in the reporting context.
visual.limitations: The frame does not show any actual gift card request, caller conversation, payment instruction, or transfer.

visual_context_notes.observation: The segment repeatedly appears as a local TV news report with Channel 5 branding and warning-style lower-thirds, rather than a direct solicitation in the sampled frames.
One visible lower-third identifies a reporter as “JESSE KNUTSON” in a newsroom setting holding a card-like object.

annotation.contextual_rationale: This video is non-scam content because it is presented as a Channel 5 report warning viewers about alleged callers who claimed to represent Microsoft. The infection warning, payment request, and gift-card repayment demand are attributed to a victim’s account and discussed for warning purposes. The news visuals and BBB payment guidance reinforce the consumer-warning context, rather than an offer of tech support by the program.
annotation.fine_grained_rationale: The primary context is an anti-scam news warning: a victim is interviewed so others will not lose money, and the report includes consumer guidance characterizing gift-card payment practices as a red flag. The alleged third-party support and refund mechanisms are depicted as conduct being reported and warned about, not as an offer by the video.
